title: ACT English: Grammar & Rhetoric in Passages
summary: The ACT English section — editing passages for grammar and effectiveness — and the rules that repeat most.

nodes.label: Underlined portions
nodes.note: Fix the underlined part or 'NO CHANGE'

chunks.heading: You're an editor
chunks.body: ACT English gives you **passages with underlined portions**; for each you choose the **best replacement or 'NO CHANGE'**. It splits into **Usage & Mechanics** (grammar, punctuation, sentence structure) and **Rhetorical Skills** (strategy, organisation, style). You're editing writing, not reading for content.
chunks.realExample: An underlined comma-splice like 'It rained, we stayed in' should become 'It rained, so we stayed in' or 'It rained; we stayed in' — you pick the option that's grammatically correct and clear.
chunks.memoryHook: You're the editor. Fix the underlined part — or pick NO CHANGE if it's already right.

chunks.heading: A handful of rules repeat
chunks.body: Most Usage questions test the **same rules**: comma use, apostrophes (its/it's), subject-verb agreement, verb tense, pronouns, and run-ons vs fragments. **Learn these few rules cold** and you'll recognise most questions instantly.
chunks.realExample: 'Its/it's' appears constantly: 'its' = possessive, 'it's' = it is. Nail that one rule and you bank easy points every test.
chunks.memoryHook: Same rules repeat: commas, its/it's, agreement, tense, run-ons. Master the few.

chunks.heading: Shorter and clearer usually wins
chunks.body: For style questions, the ACT rewards **concise, non-redundant writing**. When options say the same thing, the **shortest correct one is often right**. Delete repetition ('the reason is because' → 'because').
chunks.realExample: 'In my personal opinion, I think' is redundant — 'I think' is enough. If one option is shorter and still correct and clear, it's usually the answer.
chunks.memoryHook: When in doubt, shorter and clearer wins. Cut the redundancy.

chunks.heading: Read for the whole sentence
chunks.body: Answer each question by **reading the full sentence (and sometimes the sentence before/after)** — punctuation and pronoun questions depend on context you'll miss if you look only at the underlined words.
chunks.realExample: A pronoun question ('it' vs 'they') needs you to find what the pronoun refers back to — that noun may be in the previous sentence, so read around the underline.
chunks.memoryHook: Read the whole sentence, not just the underline. Context decides commas and pronouns.

recall.q: What do you do in ACT English?
recall.a: Edit passages — for each underlined portion, choose the best replacement or 'NO CHANGE'.

recall.q: What two broad skill areas does ACT English test?
recall.a: Usage & Mechanics (grammar, punctuation, sentence structure) and Rhetorical Skills (strategy, organisation, style).

recall.q: Which grammar rules appear most often?
recall.a: Commas, apostrophes (its/it's), subject-verb agreement, verb tense, pronouns, and run-ons vs fragments.

recall.q: When options mean the same thing, which is usually correct?
recall.a: The shortest correct and clear one — the ACT rewards concise, non-redundant writing.

recall.q: Why read the whole sentence for each question?
recall.a: Punctuation and pronoun answers depend on context (sometimes the neighbouring sentence), which you'd miss looking only at the underlined words.
